## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Adaptations of organisms to environmental conditions

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

An **adaptation** is any heritable trait — structural, physiological or behavioural — that improves an organism's survival and reproduction in its habitat. Natural selection builds them over generations: desert plants, high-altitude humans and deep-sea fish all carry solutions to the same problem (living where conditions are harsh) reached by different routes.

**Concept flow — how organisms cope with their habitat (study in this order)**

| Step | Concept | Classic example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Habitat sets the problems | Desert: heat + water scarcity; altitude: low O2 |
| 2 | Morphological adaptation | Cactus leaves reduced to spines; thick cuticle |
| 3 | Physiological adaptation | Kangaroo rat makes metabolic water; haemoglobin count rises at altitude |
| 4 | Behavioural adaptation | Desert lizards bask in sun when cold, hide in shade when hot |
| 5 | Photosynthetic specialisation | CAM plants open stomata at night (Opuntia, pineapple) |
| 6 | Mimicry and escape | Moths camouflaged on bark; desert animals active at night |

**Adaptations classified by type — with the exam examples**

| Type | Meaning | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Morphological (structural) | Body form and parts | Xerophytes: thick cuticle, sunken stomata, spines; hydrophytes: flat floating leaves, aerenchyma |
| Physiological (functional) | Internal chemistry and metabolism | CAM photosynthesis (stomata open at night); kangaroo rat's concentrated urine; increased RBC count at altitude |
| Behavioural | What the animal does | Nocturnality in desert animals; lizard thermoregulation; migration of birds |
| Reproductive | Timing and mode of breeding | Desert plants bloom after rare rains; bamboo's mass flowering |

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example — the kangaroo rat.** It lives in deserts without drinking water. Solutions: (1) physiological — its kidneys produce urine far more concentrated than ours; (2) metabolic — water released when fats are oxidised covers its needs; (3) behavioural — it stays in a cool burrow by day and feeds at night, cutting evaporative loss. One animal, three adaptation types: exactly the classification the exam asks for.

(3) How do desert lizards regulate body temperature behaviourally? (4) Compare xerophytic and hydrophytic leaf features. (5) Why do people at high altitude have more haemoglobin?

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Desert adaptations: thick cuticle/succulence (cactus CAM photosynthesis — stomata open at night), long roots, reduced leaves (spines); animals: kangaroo rat uses metabolic water, nocturnal habits — pair plant + animal.
Trick 2: Aquatic adaptations: floating leaves (water lily broad, waxy), hollow stems (buoyancy), air bladders in fish, webbed feet — the hydrophyte set.
Trick 3: Altitude adaptation in humans: more RBCs, higher haemoglobin — the physiological response line.
Trick 4: Thermoregulation classes: eurythermal vs stenothermal; homeotherms vs poikilotherms — the four vocabulary terms earn the definition marks.
